Photograph: Bill Pugliano/Getty Images Michigan University of Michigan to switch to pass/fail grades for first-semester students School said it is pivoting away from letter-grading system to ‘curb the mental health crisis’ among college students Edward Helmore Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.12 EDT Last modified on Tue 11 Aug 2026 13.31 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The University of Michigan will pivot to a pass-or-fail-style grading system, instead of letter grades, for first-semester students in an effort to “curb the mental health crisis unfolding among college-aged individuals”. The school said in a notice on Tuesday that its goal was “to help first-year students acclimate to the demands of college and allow intrinsic motivations to guide personally meaningful academic journeys” and foster “a culture of connection and collaboration – rather than competition”. Under the pilot scheme, which applies to students in the College of Literature, Science and the Arts (LSA), transcripts will show “pass or no credit”. ‘I want to be ripped to shreds’: writers flock to MFAs - but does it breed elitist literature? Read more The move comes after a mental health study across 135 US colleges and universities published last year showed lower rates of depressive and anxiety symptoms and suicidal ideation reported by students. The 2024-2025 Healthy Minds Study said symptoms of severe depression had dropped to 18% – down from 23% in 2022 – and suicidal ideation had fallen to 11%, down from 15% over the same period. Rosario Ceballo, dean of the University of Michigan, told the University Record that the decision to drop the grade system “has the potential to not only address the alarming rates of stress, depression and anxiety among our students, but to deliver on our core promise as a liberal arts and sciences college”. Timothy McKay, LSA associate dean for undergraduate education, also told the paper that the program “would provide LSA students with a smooth on-ramp as they accelerate from high school into a rigorous college education; a chance to refine their academic skills and build early momentum”. A number of universities, including the California Institute of Technology, Swarthmore College, Wellesley College and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, are also offering similar grade-covering initiatives, according to the Wall Street Journal . The changes come as universities fight to maintain standards among both students and faculty staff. In May, Harvard faculty members voted to impose a roughly 20% cap on A grades in an effort to curb decades of grade inflation that, it said, degrades the value of top-tier academic achievement at the college. The changes at Michigan come as math and science professors at the University of California in June called on regents to reinstate college-entrance exams. Students taking first-semester calculus at UC Berkeley showed “severe preparation deficits”, they said. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Around 2-3 times a day Sign up to Breaking News US Get the most important news as it breaks Preview latest after newsletter promotion “Basic mathematical fluency is analogous to literacy; without it, success in university-level Stem becomes structurally unattainable for students,” they wrote in an open letter warning that academic standards were eroding. The University of California San Diego found that the percentage of students needing remedial math classes before they could take precalculus increased to 8.5% in 2025 from 0.5% in 2020. “We now observe preparation gaps so severe that instructors must reteach middle-school mathematics while simultaneously teaching the material students need for sciences, engineering, economics and other quantitatively demanding fields,” they added. Kenneth Lowande, a former University of Michigan political science professor, told the Journal he doubted that dropping the grading system for first-semester students would make later grading any more relevant. “Grades have lost their value as an indication of quality or excellence,” he said. https://www.politico.eu/article/nato-fig.text: A Spanish F-18 fighter jet on a NATO air-policing mission Sunday shot down a drone that had illegally entered Romanian airspace. The drone was detected by radar about 24 kilometers north of the eastern city of Galați after entering Romania from Moldova. Having established radar contact, the fighter jet was authorized to shoot it down at 5:01 a.m. Authorities said debris from the destroyed aircraft had fallen in an uninhabited area between two villages. Martin O'Donnell, spokesperson for NATO operation headquarters, said additional details regarding Sunday’s incident remained under investigation but that the drone "appears to be Russian.” Advertisement Advertisement "The Ministry of National Defence is constantly monitoring the situation and informs in real time the allied structures about such events," the ministry added in a statement . It is the fourth drone shot down by NATO over Romania since the beginning of 2026. In July, Romanian F-16s downed three Russian drones that breached the country's airspace — the first such interceptions after dozens of incursions since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. In May, a Russian drone crashed into an apartment building in Galați, injuring two people. Meanwhile, Russia and Ukraine traded strikes over the weekend. Russian forces launched missile and drone attacks on Kyiv early Sunday, sparking fires in at least two districts and injuring three people, according to the city's military administration. Ukrainian drones also struck the Moscow region overnight in what the regional governor Andrei Vorobyov described as one of the largest attacks to target the area, killing an 83-year-old man.

Photograph: Reuters View image in fullscreen Survivors arrive onshore after being rescued from the capsized boat off Kyrenia, northern Cyprus. Photograph: Reuters Cyprus At least seven dead and 23 missing after ferry capsizes off northern Cyprus Authorities say 237 people rescued and search under way for those who remain unaccounted for Northern Cyprus ferry disaster – latest updates Helena Smith in Athens, Angelique Chrisafis and agencies Sun 30 Aug 2026 11.12 EDT First published on Sun 30 Aug 2026 09.14 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google At least seven people have died and 23 people are missing after a ferry carrying nearly 270 passengers and crew capsized off the coast of Turkish-occupied northern Cyprus, local authorities said. The territory’s prime minister, Ünal Üstel, told the state-run TRT news channel on Sunday that 237 people had been rescued. A search was under way for those who remained unaccounted for. “We have still not been able to reach 23 people. Search and rescue teams are working very intensively to find them,” said the Turkish ​Cypriot leader, Tufan Erhürman. “If there are people still inside the vessel, reaching them does not appear easy ‌at the moment. Efforts are being made using other technologies to reach them as well.” The ferry had “completely sunk to a depth of 514 metres”, said Erhan Arıklı, the territory’s transport minister. The catamaran-style ferry had been travelling from the port of Kyrenia, also known as Girne, in the breakaway north of divided Cyprus, to the port of Taşucu in Mersin province, Turkey. View image in fullscreen A screengrab from footage of rescued passengers. Photograph: Reuters TV/Reuters The port area of Kyrenia is a popular holiday destination for local people ⁠and tourists. The private ferry was one of several daily shuttle services that link northern Cyprus with Turkey. Mehmet Harmancı, the mayor of Turkish-held northern Nicosia, described the disaster as the worst in the more than 40 years since the territory proclaimed independence. “We’ve not seen anything like this before. It’s by far the worst tragedy. There are 23 people still missing. We think most of the passengers were Turks and Turkish Cypriots,” he told the Guardian. Hours after the ferry capsized, many details remained unclear. “We still don’t know how many have been injured or to what degree. All the injured are being brought to hospital here in [northern] Nicosia. I’m off to the hospital and am in the process of gathering warm clothes.” Kyrenia’s mayor, Murat Şenkul, said the ferry belonged to the Filo Denizcilik company and had sunk off Diana beach. It started taking in water about 7.5km (4 nautical miles) off the coast, TRT reported. Video footage from the scene showed people wearing life vests floating in the waters around the capsized vessel. When the ship capsized, passengers clung to its overturned hull. The Cyprus Broadcasting Corporation reported the boat was new and that when it began taking in water four miles from the coast, the captain had told the passengers to put on lifejackets. View image in fullscreen A rescue helicopter winches up a passenger. Photograph: Reuters TV/Reuters Erhürman told CNN’s Turkish channel he was “deeply saddened” by the loss of life. He said: “The ship capsized. It has sunk in an area where the water is 514 metres deep. So far, we have reached 244 people. Thank God, 237 of them were found alive, but seven of the people we reached have lost their lives. We have not yet been able to reach 23 individuals. Our search and rescue teams are working intensively to locate these remaining 23 people.” Speaking from the crisis centre set ⁠up in the area, he said: “There is a great sense of shock here. This is not something we have experienced before ... We are extremely saddened. Everyone is doing everything they can and making every effort.” Four coastguard vessels and a civilian passenger boat were deployed to the scene, along with five Turkish coastguard vessels and two helicopters, local officials said. Photograph: James Ross/AAP New South Wales Man charged with stabbing murder of 90-year-old woman in Bondi Beach amid spate of alleged domestic violence killings Three women were killed in separate incidents just hours apart in NSW on Saturday Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Australian Associated Press and Guardian staff Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.03 EDT Last modified on Sat 19 Sep 2026 21.15 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Three women have died just hours apart in separate incidents in one state, including an elderly woman who was fatally stabbed in an alleged domestic violence attack. A 47-year-old man has been charged with murder after the woman in her 90s was found with stab wounds inside her unit at Sydney’s Bondi Beach at about 5.15pm on Saturday. The woman was treated by paramedics but died at the scene. Police established a crime scene not far from the famous beach as detectives began investigating the circumstances. The man will appear before a bail court on Sunday. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Just hours after the death, the body of another woman in her 70s was found at Mole River in the state’s north. Police were called to reports of a domestic violence incident in the regional district about 9.35pm. Investigators believe a 37-year-old man entered a property and tried to steal a vehicle before assaulting the 74-year-old resident. The younger man was arrested and police then went on to search the neighbouring property where they found the body of a woman in her 70s, who is yet to be formally identified. Part of the house was damaged by fire, police said. A crime scene has been established at both locations and an investigation launched with help from the homicide squad. Earlier on Saturday, a 23-year-old woman was found with critical stab wounds inside a home in Wagga Wagga, in south-western NSW. Emergency services were called to the home about 11.45am but the woman died at the scene. Police were told a man left the location before officers arrived. Victorian Labor vows to close loopholes that allow domestic violence perpetrators to ‘slip through the cracks and walk free’ Read more An 18-year-old man was arrested at the scene and taken to Wagga Wagga police station, but he was later released without charge. About 8.30pm, a 31-year-old man was arrested at a home and taken to Wagga Wagga police station, where he remains. All three people are believed to have known each other. In a statement, the NSW opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said she was “horrified by the alleged stabbing deaths”. “These deaths are not isolated. According to the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, a woman was killed every 11 days in 2024-25 by her intimate partner. Even more women lose their lives when you include other family members,” she said. “Women of every age, from a 23-year-old to a woman in her 90s, are still not safe in their own homes. “Because these matters are before the courts, I won’t comment on the circumstances. But we cannot treat this as background noise. We are failing women across our country and every level of government, and every one of us, has a responsibility to act.” Explore more on these topics New South Wales Australian police and policing news Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

Photograph: Lock the Gate New South Wales Approval of biggest coal project in NSW planning commission’s history described as ‘infamous betrayal’ Independent Planning Commission says climate change impacts from Hunter Valley project will be ‘outweighed’ by economic benefits Follow our Australia news live blog for latest updates Get our new political email , free app or daily news podcast Graham Readfearn Environment and climate correspondent Wed 30 Sep 2026 01.48 EDT First published on Wed 30 Sep 2026 00.55 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The New South Wales independent planner has approved the biggest coalmine project to ever go before it, allowing mining to continue until 2045 at a Hunter Valley project described by climate groups as a “carbon bomb”. The Independent Planning Commission (IPC) has greenlit the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) Continuation Project after a contentious assessment that drew in climate and environment groups, unions, state authorities and more than 10,000 public submissions. On Wednesday, the commission said the greenhouse gas emissions from the mine, near Singleton, would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”. Locals fear for their children’s quality of life if the biggest coalmine extension in NSW is approved Read more But these impacts had been “outweighed by its benefits to the Hunter region and NSW, including continued employment, economic activity, support for local business, ongoing royalties and taxation revenue”. The IPC said the decision would “provide economic stability for the Hunter region and support a more orderly transition for workers, businesses and communities as the coal industry changes over time”. In response, Georgina Woods, the co-national coordinator of the Lock the Gate Alliance, said: “There is no other way to describe this other than a catastrophic failure of the New South Wales planning system to protect the people of the state from the worst impacts of global warming.” Climate campaigners had strongly opposed the project, saying it was out of line with Australia’s commitments under the Paris climate agreement and could affect extreme weather events. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email ‘Infamous betrayal of the public trust’ Groups reacted with dismay at the approval, with Rising Tide describing it as the “largest climate policy failure in NSW history”. The Climate Council had described the project as a “climate bomb that would supercharge climate disasters”. One of its councillors – the former NSW Fire and Rescue commissioner Greg Mullins – on Wednesday raised concerns over overseas emissions from the coal. “What NSW exports as coal, we import back as bushfires, floods, heatwaves and droughts,” Mullins said. “Climate harm does not stop at the border, and neither does the responsibility for it.” Woods said the process for considering fossil fuel projects in NSW was “the best in the country” – including with its climate change act and an independent and transparent planning authority. “The law was in place, and I am frankly shocked. It will go down in history as an infamous betrayal of the public trust.” Glencore and Yancoal – the joint owners of HVO – want to continue digging coal at the north mine site until 2045, and mine from 2030 to 2042 at the south mine. The IPC said HVO would have to prepare a plan to manage the emissions from burning the coal overseas that would limit exports to “jurisdictions with greenhouse gas emissions policies consistent with the goals of the Paris Agreement”. The project also requires federal environmental approval – a process expected to be decided before the end of the year. HVO said coal had been mined at the site for 75 years and the project, which it said had strong local support, provided jobs for 1,500 people. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion The state’s independent Net Zero Commission had warned the planning commission that approving the project could affect the state’s ability to meet climate targets in the future. Over the life of the project, the company has estimated that 809m tonnes of CO2-equivalent will be released into the atmosphere. About 794Mt of that will be emitted when the coal is burned overseas, 87% of which will come from power plants, according to presentations HVO made to the IPC. Angus Taylor pledges to repeal swathe of climate policies, saying ‘Australia has done its bit’ Read more The Net Zero Commission recommended the planning authority should consider all of the impacts from the mine’s greenhouse gases, including from the burning of the coal in power stations overseas, and pointed to advances in climate science that can attribute real-world impacts to fossil fuel projects. A new tool released by climate scientists this week suggested the additional global heating caused by the project’s approval would expose almost half a million people to unprecedented heat, kill nearly 15 million coral colonies on the Great Barrier Reef every time it bleaches and lead to more than 100 additional deaths from heatwaves in Europe to the end of this century. The NSW Nature Conservation Council’s chief executive, Jacqui Mumford, said the decision was Chris Minns’ “biggest climate failure” as premier and highlighted the government’s “complete inability to appropriately respond to the ever-growing climate crisis”. The NSW state Greens MP Sue Higginson said the approval was an “absolute betrayal of the science”, saying she “wouldn’t be surprised if the decision is challenged in the courts”. HVO said the approval “marked a pivotal milestone for 1,500 mine workers, their families and the regional economy”. It said the company was engaging with the national environmental protection agency to secure federal approval “by the end of December 2026 to continue operations”. The NSW Minerals Council urged the state government to pass legislation to limit the opportunity for a “legal challenge from climate activists determined to object to every coal mining approval on ideological grounds”. https://countercurrents.org/2026/09/ukra.text: Ukraine Before the War: Memories of a Bus Journey! in Life/Philosophy by Dr Salim Nazzal 24/09/2026 I think we sometimes need to turn away from the darkness of the news and remember happier things. Day after day, we are confronted with images of violence, destruction, and human suffering. It is difficult to watch them without feeling a certain sadness about the world we live in. So today, I want to remember a different Ukraine the Ukraine I encountered years ago. This is not a political analysis, nor is it an attempt to explain history. It is simply a human memory: an old bus crossing the polish border towards Ukrain , strangers trying to understand one another despite the barriers of language, unexpected laughter, a brief dance at a railway station, quiet villages at sunset, and distant lights appearing in the darkness. These are my memories in the bus journey to Ukrain.. 19 August 2017 A Ukrainian playwright once told me that those who travel often carry many stories with them. I find myself thinking of her words as I write on this almost-rainy morning in Oslo. I believe we need time to absorb what we have seen and heard. New places and encounters with unfamiliar people leave something within us, sometimes long after the journey itself has ended. Despite the barriers of language, we form impressions of one another. Cultures differ, customs differ, languages differ. Yet, in the end, I believe a human being remains a human being with anxieties and worries, hopes and aspirations, dreams and disappointments. I remember an elderly flower seller in Lviv who tried to convince me that good luck would come my way if I bought flowers from her. My God, what a beautiful face she had! I also remember the only Ukrainian on the bus who spoke English. His English was broken, but that did not prevent him from becoming the unofficial interpreter for my conversations with two nuns travelling with us. His translations were wonderfully amusing. Every now and then, he would confidently throw in a Ukrainian word, apparently convinced that it was English. Then there was the beautiful woman sitting alone, gazing through the window toward the distant horizon. I said to her jokingly: “You’re not going to discover America through the window!” She smiled. To my surprise, she had understood me and replied in broken English. I don’t know why, but something about her face made me imagine the faces of women celebrating after the Battle of Poltava, fought in the early eighteenth century between the forces of Peter the Great and those of the Swedish king Charles XII. When we arrived in Lviv, there was music and dancing at the station. We talked few minitues then she disappeared into the night of Lviv. Along both sides of the road stood trees dense in some places, slender in others. Their shadows stretched across the landscape like human figures standing silently as witnesses to history. How beautiful it was to watch night descend upon those villages as we travelled from Poland toward Ukraine. I have always loved looking at villages near borders. Perhaps it is because borders carry so much history. I think about the conflicts that once took place across these lands and how those struggles determined the destinies of countries and generations. It saddens me to think that so much of human history has been filled with killing and war. Around me, the Ukrainians on the bus continued talking. I understood nothing. Sometimes their voices became serious, as though they were debating something important. A few moments later, someone would say something and everybody would laugh. When we stopped at a petrol station to buy food, the young women there struck me as though they had stepped straight out of a story by Nikolai Gogol. I remembered an idea associated with Gogol’s The Government Inspector : the more closely we examine things that appear amusing, the more we begin to discover the sadness hidden beneath them. Outside, villagers walked home in the beautiful evening light. Men and women moved quietly through the landscape as though everything in the world were exactly as it should be. And yet, hundreds of miles away, there was already a war in Ukraine. I looked through the window at the enchanting sunset and the peaceful border villages, thinking about life and the strange destinies of human beings. The old bus moved like a weary horse through the Ukrainian night. One by one, the passengers fell asleep. I remained awake. I watched the darkness through the window and the faint lights of Ukrainian villages appearing in the distance and disappearing again as our old bus carried us deeper into the night. He has authored 30 books covering cultural and social issues, in addition to novels, plays, and poetry. He is the President of the European Palestinian Cultural Forum.
